identification.summary: Microsoft describes Pistachio Tempest (formerly DEV-0237) as a financially motivated actor associated with impactful ransomware distribution that experiments with different ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) offerings over time [S1]. Microsoft names Ryuk, Conti, Hive, Nokoyawa, Agenda and Mindware as payloads it has used, with Agenda and Mindware the most recent on its profile [S1]. The FIN12 name comes from the imported Microsoft naming mapping; the Microsoft profile text retrieved did not mention FIN12. Mandiant, which published the FIN12 report, describes FIN12 as a financially motivated actor behind ransomware attacks since at least October 2018, previously tracked as UNC1878 [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Mandiant: FIN12 ransomware activity since at least October 2018 [S3]. Microsoft's profile gives no first-seen date [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Pistachio Tempest (formerly DEV-0237) [S1]. FIN12 is listed as an alias in the imported Microsoft naming mapping, not confirmed on the Microsoft profile page. Mandiant says FIN12 was previously UNC1878 [S3]. This record also carries Wizard Spider, Grim Spider, TEMP.MixMaster, GOLD BLACKBURN and ITG23 from the imported Microsoft/MITRE mapping; MITRE G0102 is titled Wizard Spider [S11]. Wizard Spider (CrowdStrike) is described as the TrickBot/Ryuk/Conti operator [S5]. Whether Pistachio Tempest is the same as, a subset of, or a close partner of Wizard Spider is not stated by Microsoft's profile [S1]; Mandiant calls FIN12 a close partner of the TrickBot gang rather than the TrickBot gang itself [S4]. Keep the two clusters' facts separate; see gaps.

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered; Microsoft classes the actor as financially motivated [S1]. Mandiant assesses FIN12 is likely Russian-speaking and may be located in Commonwealth of Independent States countries [S4].
attribution.confidence: Mandiant used the qualifier 'likely' for the Russian-speaking assessment (vendor assessment, not government attribution) [S4]. Microsoft does not publish a confidence statement on its profile [S1].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry-based tracking and naming [S1][S2]; Mandiant incident-response observations of FIN12 intrusions [S3][S4]. The FIN12 alias comes from Microsoft's naming mapping, not verified on the profile page.

objectives: Financial gain through ransomware deployment, with data exfiltration and extortion also listed by Microsoft as outcomes that remain consistent over time [S1]. Mandiant reported in 2021 that FIN12 generally did not use multi-faceted extortion and appeared to prioritize speed and higher-revenue victims [S4].

targeting.notes: Microsoft lists healthcare and software and technology as targeted industries [S1]. Mandiant reported that almost 20% of directly observed FIN12 victims were in healthcare and that FIN12 activity at healthcare organizations continued before and after the October 2020 US government hospital-threat alert [S3][S4]. No regional victim breakdown was found in the sources gathered.

capabilities.summary: Initial access is typically purchased from access brokers who use existing infections from malware such as Trickbot and BazarLoader [S1]. After access, Microsoft says the actor uses Cobalt Strike alongside SystemBC and the Sliver framework, and deploys ransomware widely with PsExec [S1]. In August 2022 Microsoft named DEV-0237 as a prolific RaaS affiliate that adopted Sliver and noted that former human-operated ransomware actors were using the Bumblebee loader to deliver Sliver and other post-compromise tools [S2][S10]. Mandiant reported that FIN12 relied on Trickbot-linked initial access partners, used Cobalt Strike beacons, and mostly deployed Ryuk in 2021 [S3][S4]. The actor rotates RaaS payloads (Ryuk, Conti, Hive, Nokoyawa, Agenda, Mindware) rather than owning one ransomware family [S1].

campaigns.name: Earliest FIN12 ransomware activity (Mandiant)
campaigns.summary: Mandiant states FIN12 has conducted financially motivated ransomware attacks since at least October 2018; the cluster was previously tracked as UNC1878.

campaigns.name: Healthcare targeting around the US hospital-threat alert
campaigns.summary: Mandiant observed FIN12 activity at healthcare organizations both before and after the October 2020 joint US government alert on threats to hospitals. In the same month Microsoft and partners disrupted the Trickbot botnet, with reporting that the effect was limited.

campaigns.name: Mandiant publishes FIN12 profile
campaigns.summary: Mandiant's report describes a speed-focused ransomware actor, mainly deploying Ryuk, that relies on partners for initial access, with almost 20% of observed victims in healthcare and usually no data-theft extortion.

campaigns.name: Agenda ransomware testing (reported by S2W)
campaigns.summary: An S2W report, as relayed by search coverage, states Pistachio Tempest tested Agenda ransomware in June 2022 and suggests a possible affiliate relationship with Qilin (Agenda); this is a proposed link, not confirmed. The S2W document itself was not opened.

campaigns.name: Adoption of Sliver
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports DEV-0237 among adopters of the Sliver C2 framework, alongside or instead of Cobalt Strike, and describes Bumblebee as a loader delivering Sliver for former human-operated ransomware actors.

campaigns.name: Microsoft Pistachio Tempest profile
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's profile (dated 2024-01-25) lists Ryuk, Conti, Hive, Nokoyawa, Agenda and Mindware as payloads, with Agenda and Mindware most recent, and describes access-broker entry, Cobalt Strike, SystemBC, Sliver and PsExec deployment.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated ransomware affiliate tracked by Microsoft as Pistachio Tempest (DEV-0237) and by Mandiant as FIN12 (formerly UNC1878), assessed by Mandiant as likely Russian-speaking [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.capability: Rotating RaaS payloads (Ryuk, Conti, Hive, Nokoyawa, Agenda, Mindware); Cobalt Strike, SystemBC, Sliver; PsExec for wide ransomware deployment [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Relies on access-broker footholds from Trickbot and BazarLoader infections, and later Bumblebee-delivered tooling per Microsoft [S1][S2]. Specific C2 infrastructure is not detailed in the sources gathered.
diamond.victim: Healthcare and software and technology organizations [S1]; almost 20% of Mandiant-observed FIN12 victims were healthcare [S3].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financial extortion economy of RaaS affiliates and access brokers; no political motive is stated in the sources gathered [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise networks where pre-existing commodity malware infections can be sold on, and where administrative tools such as PsExec enable wide deployment [S1].

gaps: Cluster boundary: The FIN12 link to Pistachio Tempest rests on the imported Microsoft naming mapping and was not confirmed on Microsoft's profile page; the profile does not mention Wizard Spider [S1]. The Wizard Spider, Grim Spider, TEMP.MixMaster, GOLD BLACKBURN and ITG23 aliases in this record come from the imported mapping and MITRE G0102 [S11]; I could not open MITRE this session and did not verify the exact aliasing. Mandiant describes FIN12 as a close partner of the TrickBot gang, which suggests related but not identical operations [S4]. Do not merge Wizard Spider (TrickBot/Conti developers) facts into Pistachio Tempest without a source stating the mapping.
Microsoft gives no first-seen date, confidence statement, or victim geography [S1].

Primary documents not opened: the Mandiant FIN12 report (read only via search snippets and press coverage), the CrowdStrike Wizard Spider update, the TRM Labs analysis, and the S2W Qilin/Agenda report. Fetches to non-Microsoft hosts failed in this environment.
Mindware-specific and Nokoyawa/Hive-specific attribution to this actor rests on Microsoft's profile only; no independent incident reporting was found.
Activity after January 2024 was not found; current operational status is unknown.
No US government attribution, indictment or advisory naming Pistachio Tempest was found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Healthcare and software/technology networks are the stated target set; for DoD, relevant terrain is Military Health System, medical contractors and technology suppliers on the DIB, plus any host already infected with commodity loaders [S1]. STEP 2: The actor is an affiliate that rotates RaaS payloads, so ransomware family is a weak identifier; behavior is more stable [S1]. STEP 3: Template is purchased access from a broker (Trickbot, BazarLoader, Bumblebee-era loaders), then Cobalt Strike, SystemBC or Sliver, then PsExec-driven mass deployment, with exfiltration and extortion [S1][S2]. Mandiant noted a fast tempo [S4]. STEP 4: MLCOA is a financially driven ransomware event against a healthcare or technology organization that began as an unremediated commodity-malware infection. MDCOA is ransomware against a hospital or contractor supporting military health or logistics, where timing pressure from patient-care impact raises payment likelihood. Candidate indicators: Trickbot, BazarLoader or Bumblebee detections not remediated, new Cobalt Strike or Sliver beacons, PsExec spread across many hosts, and large outbound transfers before encryption [S1][S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track commodity-loader detections on DoD-adjacent and health-sector networks as precursors, since access is sold on before ransomware [S1]. (2) Authorities: ransomware against contractors or civilian health providers is largely outside DoD network authorities; support runs through DC3, DIB cybersecurity programs and civil agencies. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize recovery planning and offline backups for medical and logistics systems, because deployment is rapid and wide via PsExec [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators about loaders and C2 frameworks (Cobalt Strike, Sliver, SystemBC) with sector partners, and avoid naming the actor from payload alone since it rotates RaaS brands [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: Wizard Spider is a Russia-based financially motivated threat group originally known for the creation and deployment of TrickBot since at least 2016. Wizard Spider possesses a diverse arsenal of tools and has conducted ransomware campaigns against a variety of organizations, ranging from major corporations to hospitals.
